definition: Dismissive means treating something as unworthy of serious attention.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dismissive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dismissive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One dismissive glance at the demo — 'toys,' the buyer said — and he moved on to the next booth.
An unconvinced listener has weighed the case and still doubts it; a dismissive one won't put it on the scale at all.
Contemptuous goes past dismissive: the dismissive editor waves the manuscript away, while the contemptuous one makes sure you see what she thinks of you for sending it.

An offhand answer is brisk and unconsidered — tossed out mid-stride, with the mind already elsewhere. It carries no verdict. A dismissive answer carries one: the matter has been ruled unworthy of serious attention, and the brush-off is that ruling made visible.

A curt reply is short to the point of rudeness — clipped words, no warmth — yet it may still take the request perfectly seriously. Dismissive is about the verdict, not the length: however many words it spends, it treats the thing as beneath attention.

Dismissive means treating something as unworthy of serious attention.

When the apprentice glassblower floated the idea of selling the workshop's misfired pieces as seconds, the master gave a dismissive answer without looking up: 'We don't sell mistakes.' No questions, no glance at the samples she had carried in — the idea was waved off before it finished leaving her mouth.
Dismissive is the exact word because it names treatment, not just mood: the idea was treated as unworthy of serious attention — no weighing, no questions, just the brush-off.
A doubting master would have examined the samples first and then said no.
The dismissive one refuses the examining itself; the wave of the hand does all the arguing.
Dismissive describes how someone treats a thing — as unworthy of a hearing.
It pairs off with two unit-mates: disdain is the feeling of looking down, dismissive is that feeling in action, and disregard is what follows — the looking away itself.
A dismissive reply takes two seconds; its cost is whatever the unheard idea was worth.

Four members asked questions.
The fifth, Councilman Reyes, did not open the binder.
'Homework,' he said, sliding it back across the table, and moved to the next agenda item before she had sat down.
The clerk's minutes record the word most observers used afterward: dismissive — not rude, exactly, and not hurried, since he had time for every other speaker.
